He could not prevent it. What drove him frantic was the apparent certainty that Becky Thatcher had not once noticed he was still among the living. Yet she noticed well enough, knew she was winning, and enjoyed watching him suffer as she had suffered herself.

Amy’s cheerful chatter grew unbearable. Tom hinted at business demanding his attention, things that could not wait, with time slipping away. It was useless: the girl kept twittering. “Oh, bother her,” he thought, “will I never get free of her?” At last he insisted he must go and attend to those matters. She innocently promised to be “around” after school, and he hurried off, hating her for saying it.

“Any other boy!” Tom thought through clenched teeth. “Any boy in town except that Saint Louis know-all who thinks his clothes are so grand and he’s such aristocracy! All right, mister, I beat you the first day you set foot here, and I’ll do it again! Wait till I catch you outside! I’ll just—”

He acted out a beating upon an imaginary boy, striking the air, kicking, and gouging. “Oh, so you do, do you? Yelling enough now, are you? There, let that teach you!” Thus he concluded the imaginary thrashing to his complete satisfaction.

At noon Tom escaped home. His conscience could bear no more of Amy’s thankful happiness, nor his jealousy any more of the other torment. Becky returned to examining pictures with Alfred. But the minutes dragged by without Tom appearing to suffer, and her victory began to lose its brightness. Her interest faded; she grew grave and distracted, then sorrowful. Two or three times a footstep made her listen eagerly, but each hope proved false. Tom never came. Finally she felt thoroughly wretched and wished she had not gone so far. Poor Alfred, sensing without understanding that her interest was slipping away, repeatedly cried, “Oh, here’s a splendid one! Look at this!” At last she lost patience. “Oh, stop bothering me! I don’t care about them!” She burst into tears, rose, and walked off.

Alfred came alongside, intending to console her, but she said:

“Can’t you go away and leave me alone? I hate you!”

He stopped, wondering what he had done, since she had promised to look at pictures throughout the noon break. She continued on, weeping. Alfred then wandered thoughtfully into the empty schoolhouse, angry and humiliated. He soon guessed the truth: she had merely used him to work off her resentment against Tom Sawyer.

“April 12. The balloon changed direction in a remarkable way. Although I had fully expected it, the event gave me unmistakable delight. Following its previous course, it reached roughly twenty degrees south latitude, then suddenly turned eastward at a sharp angle. It continued that way all day, staying nearly, if not exactly, within the plane of the moon’s elliptical orbit. Notably, this change of course made the basket sway quite visibly. The swaying persisted with varying intensity for many hours.

“April 13. Once again I was badly frightened by the loud crackling noise that had terrified me on the tenth. I thought about it at length but could reach no satisfactory conclusion. The earth’s apparent diameter has decreased greatly: from the balloon it now covers an angle of barely more than twenty-five degrees. The moon was completely out of sight, being almost directly overhead. I remained in the plane of its ellipse, though I made little progress eastward.

“April 14. The earth’s diameter is diminishing extremely rapidly. Today I became strongly convinced that the balloon was traveling along the line of apsides toward perigee. In other words, it was following a direct course that would bring me straight to the moon at the point in its orbit closest to earth. The moon itself was directly above me and consequently hidden from view. Condensing the atmosphere demanded hard, prolonged labor.

“April 15. I could no longer trace even the outlines of continents and seas with anything approaching clarity. Around noon, I heard for the third time that appalling sound which had astonished me before. Now, however, it continued for several moments, growing more intense. Finally, while I stood stunned and terrified, expecting some unimaginable destruction, the basket shook violently. An immense flaming mass of material I could not identify roared and thundered past the balloon with the force of a thousand thunderclaps. After my fear and amazement had eased a little, I readily concluded that it was a huge volcanic fragment expelled from the world I was approaching so quickly. It was probably one of those peculiar objects occasionally found on earth and called meteoric stones for want of a better term.

“April 16. Today I looked upward as well as I could, using each side window in turn. To my great delight, a tiny portion of the moon’s disk seemed to project beyond the balloon’s enormous circumference on every side.

I cannot understand why she wanted to become close to me, but if the same circumstances arose again, I am sure I would be fooled again. Caroline did not return my visit until yesterday. In the meantime, I received no note, not a single line. When she finally came, she clearly took no pleasure in it. She gave a brief, formal apology for not visiting sooner, said nothing about wanting to see me again, and behaved so differently in every respect that by the time she left I had firmly decided to let the acquaintance end. I pity her, although I cannot help blaming her. She was wrong to single me out as she did. I can honestly say that every step toward friendship came from her. Yet I feel sorry for her, because she must know she has behaved badly, and because I am certain her concern for her brother explains it. I need not explain further. We know there is no reason for that concern, but if she feels it, it readily accounts for her behavior toward me. Since she loves her brother so much, as he deserves, any anxiety on his behalf is natural and kind. Still, I cannot understand why she has those fears now. If he cared about me at all, we would have met long ago. Something she said herself convinced me that he knows I am in London. Yet from the way she talked, she seemed to be trying to persuade herself that he truly prefers Miss Darcy. It makes no sense to me. If I were not afraid of judging too harshly, I would almost say that all this looks distinctly dishonest. I will try to put painful thoughts aside and think only of what makes me happy: your affection and our dear aunt and uncle’s constant kindness. Please write very soon. Miss Bingley mentioned that he might never return to Netherfield and might give up the house, though she spoke without certainty. We had better keep that to ourselves. I am so pleased you have good news from our friends at Hunsford. Do visit them with Sir William and Maria. I am sure you will be very comfortable there.

“Yours, etc.”

The letter caused Elizabeth some pain. But her spirits recovered when she reflected that Jane would no longer be deceived, at least by the sister. As for the brother, all hope was now completely gone.
